Question: What does Balaji Viswanathan think about Donald trump's H1B visa bill? How could it effect the IT sector in India and is it preferable to pursue MS in USA after this bill?
Answer: Would love for Dr. Balaji Viswanathan (பாலாஜி விஸ்வநாதன்) to answer this. Meanwhile a similar question was answered on Quora here. I’ll paste my answer from there: tl;dr: If it passes the way it is worded, the bill will reduce the pool of available visas to Indian IT firms. But 130K is not the minimum wage those clickbait headlines make it to say; that’s something different. Let me explain First, some background: 1. Indian IT firms are very large users of H1B In fact, some would say, that they are the biggest users. e.g. see here: Indians got 86% of the H1B visas for tech firms issued by the US in 2014 - The American Bazaar 2. There is wide-spread myth in the US about “H1B workers taking jobs” from Americans Jobs are outsourced due to cost-savings of globalization, not due to H1B. For every IT worker Indian companies bring to US, there are 10 that are back in India, doing the work. Sponsoring H1B visas is also expensive viz. $8–10K, and the whole point of outsourcing is not to increase costs. It’s hence in the interest of IT companies to bring as few workers as possible. But there is just so much work outsourced and massive cost savings thereof. Yes, some American workers do lose their jobs, but it’s because of reduced costs due to globalization, and not because of H1B. e.g. if a company outsources 100-workers’ worth work to India, the work of 80 of those 100 workers will now be done offshore, and not in US. Only about 20 workers’ worth of work will be done locally, which may be displaced by H1B workers. Also, note that most of those 100 jobs, are relatively low-skilled jobs. Do you really think a company is going to outsource their most important jobs to overseas people? However, whenever even few jobs are lost, it gets a lot of bad press and complains to the lawmakers’ offices. A little too much of it. That is what prompts legislators to bring these reform acts. After all, they also want to feel relevant, like all of us are. Now let’s analyze the bill in some detail Here is the current wording of the bill, for the curious, patient and frustrated: https://lofgren.house.gov/upload... At first, I was shocked, when I read that “minimum is 130K” headlines. But when I dug into it more, I realize that 130K is not what it means. H1B dependent employers are employers with at least 15% workers that are H1B dependent. Turns out, most Indian IT firms are not H1B dependent employers. See here: H-1B-dependent employer - Wikipedia . There are intricate ways of calculating and attesting that, and the bill doesn’t address any of that. [Edit: A couple of readers pointed out, that many Indian IT firms are indeed classified as H1B dependent. For this, a more reliable source than Wikipedia is: Solution for Work Visa, Student Visa, Visa Jobs and Green Card . Note though, there too, you will still find some LCA applications from the same employers, which are filed indicating no H1B dependency. That may be a mistake on their part] It simply means, that if you don’t want to pay that much, you have to fill out some extra paperwork viz. “attestations” that you won’t do such and such things. All those “things” to be attested/promised are very fluffy and difficult to prove. And have been around since the 90s. This bill doesn’t address any of that. Language includes doing a “market based compensation”, including “cash bonus” and “other similar compensation”. It’s anyone’s guess how this can be gamed. This bill doesn’t pay attention to that. In other words, no “130K” isn’t too relevant to Indian IT firms. What may affect the Indian IT firms The thing that may affect IT companies, is the intent of the bill to do “market based” allocation. e.g. if some employer is willing to pay 200% of wage, they will get a preference in allocation. In order to reduce costs, IT firms will very likely not pay very high salaries to H1B workers they bring here, and thus may lose those visa applications to other employers willing to pay higher. Reservation of 20% of quota for small employers will also reduce the pool of available visas for these big firms. Plus, the minimum wage tier has also been removed, which will increase costs for the IT firms. However, writing was on the wall for a number of years and these firms have already anticipated this tightening. They have hence moved a lot of their visa allocation to L1 visas. The bill doesn’t address the real issue The way it is, falls short in a number of ways in addressing real problems. Apart from the ones I mentioned earlier, the other real issue, is the power imbalance between the employer and the employee. The employer has just so much influence on the job and say on the career of the employee, that you can easily find H1B employees stuck working for same employers for years together, with low salaries. The other thing influencing condition of H1B workers, is the one following and bigger mess viz. Green Cards, which has ridiculousness of its own. That is also not addressed by this bill. Finally, there are multiple such bills So this is not the only H1B reform bill. While this is the most jazzy of all reform bills bill, there are multiple bills. We don’t know which bill will be discussed/enacted. If you are in the US or planning to come to US, your best bet is to work for some of the top employers. e.g. Google, Facebook, etc, who have offices all around the world. Work hard to get in there, get treated fairly, get paid very well, and make an amazing career without worrying about this political mess.

Question: Is there life after a data structures course?
Answer: Nope. Not in this world anymore. But regret not - you will get reincarnated in a new world! Alphabetical lists will become sorted arrays to do a binary search. Never again, will you scan a list of names. It will be searched, one half at a time. If it is unsorted, then you will proudly take the high road and refuse to look up. A trip to a grocery store will be a quest for the shortest path. So will be finding a parking spot. And of course, only if the store manager knew of lookup tables, so that you won’t have to scan that entire damn isle for your favorite cereal. Pringles anyone? Pop one at a time from the stack, for it’s impossible to do it any other way. Back home, those pesky children are merely forks, really. Smalltime structures, not useful to handle real-world scale. Sometimes recursive. Why even play silly things like Jigsaw puzzles with them? Those are just backtracking problems. Even Sudoku. Don’t waste your time, lousy kids! Just write some loops and it solves itself. Ex calling? What? How can that be? We’re now such disjoint sets! Remember the fight we had when I argued that killing children is a perfectly normal thing to do? Yes, you just wait for them and if they don’t return, you just look them up by their IDs (who needs names?) and kill them. That’s what’s normal in CS. Standing in line for a movie ticket will also feel so normal. After all, it’s just FIFO. Though finding that the movie theatre is full will be a source of instant regret, for it is a lousy data-structure that can’t be dynamically resized! What agony. Back home again, trimming that tree is just an act of rebalancing. An upside down structure, that too. Did I tell you that backyards will merely become memory storage with pointers to trees? Hunting for an apartment? A graph problem, really. Thanks Dijkstra and every other person who already optimized it for me. Doesn’t really matter what apartment it is, as long as it’s found the most efficient way. Writing answers on Quora? Why do these muggles type paragraphs and paragraphs? Everything just needs to be a list. Then it can be traversed, instead of read. Welcome to the new world, a world where everything now is a quest for (data) structure and … simplicity :-) [Source: Years of training others in Data Structures and Algorithms for Challenging interviews: Interview Kickstart]

Question: What lame things do programmers often argue about?
Answer: Programmers (claimer: I’m one) tend to argue about a lot of lame things (tabs vs spaces, placement of braces, naming of variables, number of return statements, parameter passing etc). But know that bickering on lame things is not a privilege of programmers. There are parallels in every profession. So much so, that unlike other kinds of bickering, this even is a named law for it! It’s very appropriately called the Law of Triviality. Quoting Wikipedia: Parkinson's law of triviality is C. Northcote Parkinson's 1957 argument that members of an organisation give disproportionate weight to trivial issues. He observed that a committee whose job was to approve the plans for a nuclear power plant spent the majority of its time on discussions about relatively minor but easy-to-grasp issues, such as what materials to use for the staff bike-shed, while neglecting the proposed design of the plant itself, which is far more important but also a far more difficult and complex task. The law has been applied to software development and other activities. The term bike-shedding or the bike-shed effect was coined as a metaphor to illuminate the law of triviality; it was popularised in the Berkeley Software Distribution community by the Danish computer developer Poul-Henning Kamp in the mid-1990s and has spread from there to the whole software industry. Poul-Hemming Kamp even has an almost entertaining and emotional webpage for it: bikeshed.com. If you refresh that page, you will get a different background color each time. I like blue. It’s the best. All other colors are the worst. Blue makes everything better. How can you not see that? You’re colorblind. Now refresh that page! Again. Wait for blue.

Question: I have a Google onsite interview coming. They wanted me to sign a paper with the employment history and the current salary. Should I disclose the current salary?
Answer: Realize, that: 1. Your salary at any company (let alone Google) is a function of many many things, most of which are not under your immediate control. Many things = your interview performance, your experience, budgets, importance of the team you are joining, salary of your peers, the bonus and equity component etc. 2. Well-run companies like Google understand, that talent is their core-competence and they won't skimp on salaries. Saving a few K in your salary is not going to make a substantial difference to Google. 3. If you don't have a competing offer, you really don't have a clear negotiation advantage. Mentioning your salary upfront or not, is not going to move the needle much. Before you go into such negotiation, you need to have a good sense of what the typical salaries are at Google (check Glassdoor, salar.ly, etc) in your area. If you cannot get that information, then you need at at least have a sense of current overall market salary for your region. Once you have that, I'd just clearly state the facts: 1. If your current salary is lower than market, put this note on the side: "My current salary is X, which is below market. I'm expecting to be paid at market in my next job" 2. If your current salary is higher than market, put this note: "My current salary is X, which is a bit higher than market. I'd like to maintain or beat that in my next job" Hope this helps!

Question: Are there really engineers making 300k+ in Silicon Valley?
Answer: It is the truth. Not just $300K, but much more than that. $500K, $600K, $1MM+… Per year. How do I know? What kind of companies make these offers? Every company that values technical talent very highly, is willing to make these offers. They have to, because they are competing with each other for the same talent. Company size/stage doesn’t matter. Tiny companies have made these offers and giants have too. Location doesn’t matter these days either. Most of these are colocated in California, NY, and Seattle, but we’ve seen these in Michigan and Oklahoma too. Both, tech and non-tech companies have given out these offers. e.g. Ford, a manufacturing company of many generations, has now realized that without self-driving, they are doomed. They are now willing to pay top dollar for that talent. When the leadership values core tech as a critical part of the business, they will open up the wallet. How much experience is required to get these offers? Generally, we see such high offers only for experienced engineers. About 5 years+ of software development experience is required. It is rare for fresh/recent grads (and for new entrants into programming) to get these numbers, unless of course, you come with a strong pedigree e.g. Stanford CS. No, you don’t need a PhD, or even an MS. Is it all cash? No. Up to about $500K, it’s usually half cash (including bonus), half equity. Beyond that, equity dominates. Equity may not feel as exciting as cash, but consider this: How do I prepare to get these offers? (which I think, is the real question you’re asking): A few months of hard work, a lifetime of gravy. It’s the best of times; it’s the worst of times. [To put this into perspective, 75% of America has saved less than $200K for their entire retirement. Here, we’re talking about 2x to 5x that every year. And this has been going on for at least a decade.]

Question: Out of general aptitude, knowledge in datastructures and algorithms, coding skills and culture fit, which one is most important for a candidate to be selected in software engineering role?
Answer: I once interviewed a candidate who came from a respectable CS college i.e. he clearly had general aptitude. I asked him a warmup question involving a BST. He solved it well, clearly demonstrating that he had “knowledge” of that particular data structure. He also coded it correctly, demonstrating that he “knew” coding. I then took it further, and gave him a problem where the input dataset required to be put into a BST in order to efficiently find a target element. He couldn’t solve that. After I gave him plenty of hints, he got it. But when he proceeded to code it, he fumbled and ended up with some basic bugs. Nice guy, we all liked him as a person. But did not get hired. So there you go - this one had all: general aptitude, knowledge of DS/Algos, coding skills and culture fit. But they didn’t culminate into the most important skill of all: Problem Solving. Question: What might it be called in computer science where we have a tree structure where any given node can have 3 children (a left, middle and right child)? In my case, opening and closing tags, and then stuff that can go between/middle of those tags.
Answer: Are you looking for a Ternary Tree? Ternary tree - Wikipedia And of course, like John L. Miller suggested, in general, a tree with at most K nodes (children) at every node, is called a K-ary tree. A ternary tree is a special case of a K-ary tree. Before using a Ternary tree though, think hard if you actually need one. I obviously do not know your use-case, and whether it’s only academic, but I’ve often seen people tending to use a ternary structure when a binary would suffice. A common mistake is to create a third (or middle) node for something that can simply go as an attribute (value) of existing nodes.

Question: How do I tell my interviewer that ''I don't know that but I can easily look it up in the web?” I'm conceptually weak, but when a given a task and some time I can achieve good results. I learn by diving into the problem directly. How do I sell myself?
Answer: Think about it. Question never is whether you can simply learn something new. Those who want, will, when put on a problem, given enough time. Question always is - how quickly can you learn in that time? How deep can you go in the same time compared to others? And in the process, do you get along with everyone else, or do you cause too much collateral damage? This is what interviewers are trying to find out in an interview, at the very core of it. To do things fast, conceptual clarity is critical to have. Having prior conceptual clarity gets you closer to “good results” faster. And in the same amount of time, it moves you further from just “good results” to “great results” (deeper). So while I’m glad you admitted your weakness, you shouldn’t stop there. Strive to seek conceptual clarity before you try to sell yourself. Yes, seeking conceptual clarity is not easy. It’s hard work, but is entirely worth it.

Question: Am I "owed" interview feedback? I interviewed at Facebook and thought it went well, but they sent me a form rejection letter and didn't respond to my polite request for feedback. I don't want to keep making the same mistakes. Is that unreasonable?
Answer: It was 2007, and I was at eBay. I was conducting a technical phone-screen. The candidate wasn't doing particularly well with the questions. After about 45 minutes, I wrapped it with these words: "Hey, it was great talking to you!", put my notes into the system, and then went on with my daily stuff. What followed, was somewhat hilarious and bizarre. After the candidate got his rejection, he was furious. He called HR and asked why he was rejected, even though "the interviewer said it was great talking to me!". He couldn't make sense of the fact that it was simply a courtesy and even though it was indeed great talking to him, that didn't mean he did well in the interview. The recruiter had to go take permission from the lawyer before sending him my (redacted) feedback. But that didn't pacify him either. He went over the recruiter's head, to his manager and everyone he could find. He persisted for several weeks with one silly reason or another, demanding "the answer". Eventually, the position got filled with an internal transfer, after which he stopped. Isolated case, you say? Of course. But look at how much time and effort we had to sink into it. That's the tragedy with giving feedback (and many other things in life). 1% of isolated irrational cases take 99% of time and 101% of mindshare. Sorry, however genuine your reason is, and however well meaning the interviewers are, a fair system of giving feedback unfortunately just doesn't scale (and we must create something that works at scale). Don't expect it; you're not owed any. PS: Realize that even colleges don't give us feedback when they reject us. That, despite taking an application fee. And despite us having spent years trying to get into one. PPS: Nobody owes you feedback even when you clear the interview. Most people don't care about feedback on success, but the point is, that it's very hard to give feedback even when it's positive. The right way to look at an interview, is like a date, and not like a standardized test. The more you think about interviews like the latter, the more you will agonize about feedback and scoring and such. It doesn't work that way. [Major edits: Added PS and things after that]

Question: What percentage of software engineers that have already been matched to a team make it through the Google hiring committee?
Answer: It looks like Google has recently been experimenting with its hiring process, at least when it comes to experienced software engineering positions. Earlier, all candidates had to be blessed by the Hiring Committee (HC) before the team matching phase. Now, for many candidates, they have switched the order of these two steps. i.e. Given your interview performance and profile, they first see if there is enough interest from a team at Google, and only with that blessing, the recruiter takes the profile to the HC. If no team at Google wants to take a chance on the candidate, then the profile may be forwarded to HC as is, but then the chances of them getting thru HC are less, despite a good interview. Exactly how long a recruiter waits for team matching to happen before conceding, is largely driven by how long the candidate can wait, and what’s reasonable. We’ve seen people wait up-to 3 months, and we’ve seen immediate matches also. If some team at Google wants to take a chance, then the HC takes that into serious consideration when reviewing interview feedback and delivering the verdict. Exactly why and how the process change has been implemented, when did it start, and for how many, is not something that’s possible to know/guess from outside.

Question: Why are so many software engineering interviews just ridiculously and unnecessarily difficult (not just Google)?
Answer: That’s because those questions actually reflect the kind of work the company does. But you’re right - not all companies do that kind of work; only some do. Even at Google and Facebook, which are known of some of the most ground-breaking technical innovations in this generation, many many (most even) teams don’t do work that’s nearly as intellectually challenging as the interview questions they ask. So the real question is, why do they and some other companies, ask such questions for nearly all their software engineering roles? Following is the underlying corpus of reasons that compels most companies to do so: 1. Wherever possible, companies want to standardize the hiring bar across the entire department If companies don’t do that, then it can quickly get pretty chaotic. Some teams will feel superior to others and vice-versa. Internal mobility of engineers will become a lengthy and difficult process. They won’t be able to switch programming languages/stacks/tools that fluently. Each team will get a license to become a technical fiefdom, which will slow down the entire development process. Standardizing the hiring bar pre-solves for a number of problems in a short time. But then the question is, why standardize to challenging questions? 2. Without challenging questions, it’s slow and difficult to hire for many open positions in short time Most of these companies do such good work and pay so well, that they have a very strong pipeline of engineers applying to them. At Box, for example, it was routine to have hundreds of submissions for many open positions. If we threw easier questions in interviews, it would have rendered our entire tiered process useless (phone screens to onsites). After all, it is impossible to compare engineering capabilities of two engineers both of who can these days flawlessly reverse a string, and design a web-page with 3 buttons. (Granted, there are some companies who don’t have such strong pipelines, and/or are not hiring for so many positions and/or also not doing challenging work. Those companies should consider switching to a lighter interview process) But then the question is, how are so many engineers able to solve such problems? 3. Companies know, that candidates do targeted preparation for interviews, so the difficulty of questions has continued to inch higher Candidates have been preparing for technical interviews for 20+ years. First serious book (the most basic means of targeted preparation for anything) to come out and expose programming interviews was in year 2000. In last 17+ years, that landscape now has more seminal books, online judges, websites, sophisticated testing tools, ad-hoc meetups and even serious bootcamps[1] like ours. 4. Companies just want to have very driven engineers in all corners, and they can afford to Companies often only want to hire engineers who are capable of solving challenging problems, whether they actually have such problems on not. That’s because the belief is that the same engineers will often solve the mundane problems more innovative-ly and possibly at a different level of abstraction. They have to pay these gals and guys more, of course, because all competitors are vying for the same engineers. But that’s okay - they can afford it. They are either profitable like Google, or have easy access to VC money. At the end of the day, many of us just want to work with very driven people on whichever problems that are thrown at us. If a company can attract those people (like you and I!) and afford to pay them, then why won’t they do it? This apparently ridiculous and unnecessary process is working This process has been around for 30+ years largely in the same form (DS/Algos). Microsoft glorified it, then Google took the baton and now Facebook has carried it to yet another level. Many of these gals and guys at these companies are some of the most driven, most savvy and most impatient people on the planet. If something doesn’t work for them, they fix it in 30 minutes and don’t sit on it for 30+ years. But they haven’t even touched it. And they won’t. With a thousand foot pole. Because it works. You don’t like it? Guess what - your neighbor is willing to put up with it. Companies just want their problems solved. Doesn’t matter who solves them. If it’s not you, then it’s going to be someone else. I guarantee it.

Question: What are the biggest mistakes engineers make when they interview?
Answer: This answer is directed towards software engineers, but some of the tips apply equally well to other engineers. The biggest strategic mistake, by far, is that the candidates interview with a loaded agony of getting a job, instead of simply demonstrating who they are. See, when you're agonizing about getting that job, you'll be nervous, you'll judge yourself during the interview, you'll amplify small mistakes, you'll fumble. But when you go there to simply explore, simply to solve a fun problem, to see how far you yourself can get, and to respect the interviewer's time, you will notice that most fumbling starts to go away. You'll take control of the interview then, because you're not agonizing. Like Bryan Cranston says: there is power in that. If you haven't watched the following clip, it's worth watching, over and over again. He is talking about actors and audition, which is very similar to interviewing: The other big strategic mistake, is actually made before the interview viz. they under-estimate the amount of preparation required. They walk into an interview like it's a lottery ticket, surprised why they didn't win it. There are some other big tactical mistakes also: 1. Not realizing that half the interview is about your communication and behavior in the interview. Had communication and behavior not been important, the companies would just send you some coding problems to do, and generate an automatic offer letter after test-cases passed. But no company does that. Why? Because they want a conversation, and you have to be ready for an inspiring conversation. 2. Trying to go for the most optimal solution from the get go, and overlooking to give the brute force. If you can't think of an optimal solution, and you don't give a brute-force solution either, the interviewer keeps wondering if you even understood the problem. Remember, that an interview is a date; it's not a standardized test. It's about showing who you are, and not about agonizing about fitting into someone's mould. You will make far less mistakes when you recognize the true nature of the beast. [I run Coding Interview Bootcamp for a living. We help candidates prepare to crack into some of the best tech companies]

Question: Is it only me who thinks that the "Rate yourself in X skill" is the worst question one can ask in an interview?
Answer: I think that the intent of the asker is right, but it's a poorly presented question. They want to know how much you've worked in X skill and absorbed it. That's fair. But if they want you to rate yourself on a scale, they need to present an objective scale. e.g. Someone once asked me to rate myself on C++ and immediately followed it with this: 1 means you haven't touched it, 5 is where you've written a decent amount of professional code and 10 is where you've contributed to the spec. If they don't give you some explanation of the scale, you can start your answer with: "Well, rating on a scale is subjective, but if I create a scale that looks like this and this, then this is where I fall" OR "I don't know how to rate myself on it, but I can tell you what kind of work I've done. I've written about 3000 lines of code in C++ a couple of years ago, where I used STL extensively. I have once needed to refer to the spec, but that's about it. Now what do you think is my rating?"

Question: What do interviewers look for when interviewing software engineering candidates?
Answer: An interviewer is usually evaluating you for three things: i) Do you have the skills? ii) Are you a problem solver? iii) Are you someone I/my team can work with? A tech interview can take between 45 minutes to an hour. Over an hour is generally a good sign. One of the first things that will be noted is your demeanor, and the interviewer will pick on any hints they get - are you shy, timid, confident, involved, apathetic etc. Unless the interviewer wants to jump in straight away (this happens often and can throw you off), there will be some small talk that may involve a couple of tricky questions like: - I haven't had a chance to look at your resume. Can you fill me in on the highlights? - How do you think your other interviews have gone? (If you've had other interviews with the team before this one.) The first question has several variations (“Tell me something about yourself.”) and you’re likely to have been asked a few (100?) times if you've given many interviews. It's important to make sure that your answer is crisp and short. Don't ramble on about where you went to school and other obvious details from your resume. Instead, make it a story that talks more about what lies between the lines on your resume - what your experience has taught you, an example of a tough problem you've solved, what you could bring to the table or even the team you are interviewing with. The second question is trickier. Your personal perception of how things went might be completely different from feedback the interviewer may have already received before walking into the room. The easiest way to tackle this is, to be honest without being either emphatic or vague. You may want to avoid a response like, "They went great" or "I think I killed it". But neither should you take the other extreme, with an "I did terrible in <insert round/problem>". Keep it as neutral, like this: "I think I solved the first question on finding the longest subsequence well but stumbled a little bit on the design problem. I think I could have done better with a little more time." These questions offer the interviewer useful insights about you, and convey the impression that you are secure and comfortable with the good and the bad, and more importantly, that you are the sort of person they'd like to work with. On to the main course - the technical questions. Technical interviewers generally bring two questions to the table. The first: A coding problem to test your knowledge of fundamental data structures and algorithms, something they expect you to solve reasonably quickly (say in 20 mins). The second: A more abstract question that tests your ability to break down a problem and identify a way to solve the problem. This could be a system design question (Design YouTube) or a more focussed question (Design data models for a video streaming service that should be able to stream to multiple devices and support up to a billion users a month). Your interview is usually over if you struggle with the first question. We may not be exposed to core data structures and algorithms in our day job but top companies use that as a minimum benchmark to move you ahead in the interview process. These problems usually test your knowledge of time and space complexity (think Big "O"), your ability to quickly assess what is efficient (and inefficient), and most importantly to write clean code on the whiteboard/coding platform being used. Your evaluation on the second question is mostly based on - How quickly do you break a problem down and figure out what pieces need more clarification? - What follow up questions do you ask the interviewer to get more information? - How well can you articulate your thought process? - Your ability to make tradeoffs and to justify them. - Your ability to offer ballpark estimates for memory, disk space, network load, buffer sizes, etc. The deeper you get into the second question, the better your interview is going because you are challenging the interviewer to throw more at you. On both technical questions, you are being evaluated for all of these: - Articulating your thoughts (GOOD) - Rambling contradictory thoughts (BAD) - Follow up questions and telling the interviewer the direction you are going (GOOD) - Long unexplained silence (BAD) - Organized whiteboard showing assumptions, estimates and linking them to how you are solving the problem (GOOD) - Completely messy whiteboard with no coherence (BAD) - Interviewer throwing newer and more challenges at you than hints (GOOD) - The opposite of the above (BAD) The key to all of these interviews is to be prepared. Companies, at least the coveted tech companies, expect you to prepare before their interviews. It is important to give yourself enough time to practice hard and solve as many different types of questions, know your resume in detail and hone your personal narrative well enough to give yourself the best chance. If you are looking for a structured way to prepare for interviews, take a look at Interview Kickstart.

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: What are your greatest frustrations/challenges when studying data structures/algorithms and prepping for technical interviews? What are your biggest roadblocks to learning and retaining knowledge?
Answer: Congratulations. Everyone keeps complaining that algorithms and Data Structures are hard, but very few dig deeper to ask why. And only those who do, actually get better at it (or actually can help get others better at it). Let's think about it, shall we? First of all, let's realize that learning in itself, is a problem in NP. i.e. while it's possible to verify whether you've learnt something in a bounded, explainable (polynomial) amount of time, nobody really knows how to achieve learning. The teaching community has their best empirical guesses crystallized over a period of time, but there is no theoretical universal systematic pattern that has been established. i.e. you won't be able to tell me today with 100% certainty, that if you read/do X and Y, you will learn Z. You'll be able to test me on Z and be clearly be able to tell if I have learnt Z, but you won't be able to tell how I exactly got there, and be able to replicate that pattern with others. That's just how complex each human mind is. Now back to the questions: you are asking three separate but related, very good questions here: Question 1: What do you feel are the biggest roadblocks to learning and retaining knowledge, understanding, and implementation details of algorithms and data structures? I first-hand connect with this problem from several angles. I've had trouble learning algorithms, I've had trouble in hiring engineers, I've had trouble in preparing candidates for CS interviews AND I've had trouble in finding instructors who can do so. I divide the roadblocks into two categories: A. System Roadblocks and B. Thinking Roadblocks A. System Roadblocks aka Roadblocks in setting up a system of learning. The key to learning anything new (especially cognitively challenging tasks like Algorithms), is to persist with it for long enough time, under proper guidance, with challenging curriculum and motivated peers. That system is probably more important than the topic itself. If you are in the right school, then you get all of that in a package. If you're not, then all those things become roadblocks. Roadblock-1: Finding engineers/teachers who can give proper guidance Books are a great source, but having someone knowledgeable to ask questions is critical to speedy and long-term learning. And of course, by definition, there are aren't that many people who know Algos/DS stuff well enough, that they can guide others. Roadblock-2: Finding peers who want to learn it with the same seriousness We all know, that learning something together is not only fun, it's also fast and we retain things longer. But having the right partner is important. You need someone who is at the same level as you, and is committed just like you are. Otherwise it's a serious waste of time and leads to demotivation. Roadblock-3: Absence of enough real-world projects There are not many real world projects today that require you to select or implement algorithms or DS. (Why? See one of my answers Soham Mehta's answer to I've been coding for some time now and have developed several web applications. I haven't used any algorithms or even much math. I haven't done any of the complicated things that are so often talked about in computer science. Why?) When you are not faced with many real-world applications of what you're learning, it's very easy to get demotivated. Not to mention, that without an existential pressure to do something, it's very hard to learn something new properly. A hitler parody is in order:  B. Thinking Roadblocks (or frustrations) Roadblock-4: Too much exposure to linear thinking The way humans learn, they associate everything new with something that's very familiar to them. The real world forces us to think linearly all day, because that's how nearly everything works. viz. this happens after that, 4 comes after 3, etc. When it comes to Algos and DS though, there is much more than linear thinking. There is looping, there is recursion, there are trees and then there is memoization. All of these are not very natural constructs for the world that's mostly linear. But we have a habit of associating every Algo/DS linearly, which holds us back (roadblock). That's why you'll notice that most people are good with Arrays and Linked Lists, but complain about nearly everything else. Roadblock-5: Not having cultivated mathematical thinking What is mathematical thinking? Mathematical thinking (not necessarily mathematics) makes a lot of CS easier. Mathematical thinking is about recognizing patterns. It's about organizing your thoughts to create something. e.g. Take the question: what is the sum of positive integers from 1 through N? This is high-school math. But if one doesn't remember the formula, then one should be able to derive it. The moment you put 1 thru N on the board, a pattern should jump out, leading you to the answer. Such thinking only develops thru proper grade-schooling and again, deliberate effort. A lack of it makes CS learning slow, and Algorithmic/Data-Structure interviews even slower. Roadblock-6: Not enough patience/time Learning anything new needs you to struggle with it, break your world views and then wrestle it down to the ground. Many people don't have the time or patience to do so. Roadblock-7: Not enough revision Recall is as important as learning. IOW, it's not enough to just learn something; it's also enough to practice recalling it, or you may not be able to recall it when the time comes. Revision and repetition are key. Roadblock-8: Rarely, some people just don't have the mind for it See this study if you haven't: Hitting the High Notes "The quality of the work and the amount of time spent are simply uncorrelated." Quesion-2: Why do so many interviewees have trouble with technical interviews? Assuming this question is limited to Algos and DS, the answer to this now becomes simple: 1. They haven't studied CS properly in college They have CS degrees (bachelors, masters, doesn't matter), but they coasted for the most part, doing just enough to pass the exams and maintain a GPA. They did not take time to really persist through difficult problems. They did not surround themselves with peers who would study together and challenge each other. Their teachers did not pay enough attention either. A great example is understanding of Recursion. Most people struggle with recursion when they do it first, but only those who persist through several problems, internalize it and retain it for a long time. 2. OR once they are out of school, they have not been able to overcome the roadblocks mentioned above See the list of roadblocks identified above. Most people want to win, but they don't have the will to prepare to win i.e. the will to remove the roadblocks to winning. 3. They have practiced properly, but the company hasn't thought properly about their interviewing process Many interviewers tend to ask what they know, vs. what's required for the job. If the interviewee is not in the interviewer's window of knowledge, then they will be perceived as lacking. This often happens with inexperienced interviewers. Yet another set of interviewers don't put in enough effort in picking out questions that are relevant for the job. They treat interviewing like it's intellectual perversion. Many companies don't have a culture of paying attention to interviewing. See one of my other answers here: Can candidates in programming interviews really write code on the spot?  Also, a Dilbert strip is in order: Dilbert comic strip for 02/14/1993 from the official Dilbert comic strips archive. 4. They are a mismatch from the get-go Some just pick wrong companies to interview with, even though their backgrounds don't match. Companies also overlook this fact quite often. e.g. if I interview at a Semiconductor company, it's not likely that I'll pass that interview. Question 3, the one you're really asking: Why wouldn't interviewees learn Algos and DS and prepare for interviews? 1. They don't know or can't admit, that they will have to practice Best way to practice, is to keep working a little bit on the side while you're on the job and that it can be done. See some amazing answers to this question: How can I get a job at Facebook or Google in 6 months? I need a concise work-plan to build a good enough skill set. Should I join some other start-up or build my own projects/start-up? Should I just focus on practicing data structures and algorithms? If they knew or admitted, they'd look for ways to make it happen. 2. They prepare, but not deliberately Anything you need to get good at, needs Deliberate Practice. Interviews are no different. In order to confidently prepare before walking into a challenging interview, one needs to do some of the following things: a. Time himself/herself when coding b. Do mock interviews c. Work on the right programming problems (not too easy, progressively harder) d. Work with a teacher or an expert who can guide e. Follow a process that encourages recall as effectively as learning of new concepts f. Struggling with difficult problems until they are completely solved g. Have the right solutions to learn from and apply to h. Have the right, optimistic mindset i. Do enough number of problems j. Be in similar company and exchange ideas k. Read the right books and prior work As you can see, a lot of things need to come together to overcome difficulties and increase retention. 3. They prepare, but not with a competitive mindset In an interview, it's not enough to be good at Algorithms and DS. You also have to be competitively good i.e. solve those problems under time-pressure. Interviews are a competition. But most daily programming jobs don't require you to program competitively in a time-bound manner. Programmers are not athletes; they are creative people. But interviewing is meant for athletes. That's because as a hiring manager, I only have budget for one position and only so much time. I'm hence going to make all the candidates run (program) as fluently as they can in a given amount of time. Which means, that to succeed in that race, one needs to practice competitively on the side, to keep up with fast thinking. And most people are either unaware or too lazy to do that. 4. They are practicing, but are using your interviews to "practice" Some candidates knowingly do "practice" interviews with companies they don't care much about, before they interview with their favorite companies. 5. They overvalue their experience Research has shown for a number of years, that software engineering is not a field where experience necessarily turns into expertise. World is divided into two kinds of tech companies: Ones that deal with Scale (Google, Facebook, Twitter etc.) and ones that don't. (Scale == Millions of users). The former kind deal with enough challenging problems, that needs their engineers to pay enough attention to every part of the code. Otherwise, the site gets very slow and grinds to a halt. Those engineers end up getting exposed to several algorithmic techniques and data-structures in that environment, and hence have bit of an easier time interviewing outside. Not to mention that they also get exposure to such interview questions where they work. Working at companies (or teams) that don't deal with Scale does make for well paying careers, but often doesn't expose you to problems challenging enough to warrant a better data-structure and algorithm. Candidates coming from those companies hence, often struggle. If you have not been working at a company that throws such problems at you every day, there is no chance you're going to do well in interviews without explicit practice. 6. They think it's okay to be good-enough, and high demand will work in their favor The demand for tech talent is just so high. Most people know that they are going to find something or the other, so they don't care if they fail a few interviews. It may not be at your company; but some other company. That reflects in their performance in your interviews. They hence try to throw a lot of spaghetti on the wall to see what sticks. -- Phew! That got a little too long. Hopefully it's useful!

Question: What are the interview design questions which do not fall into the system design category?
Answer: Categorization in interview-questions’ landscape, is a bit random. It’s often not possible to clearly tell what is a “system design” question and what is a “coding” question. * Take Concurrency for example. It’s a “system design” question in some ways, because you’re designing a concurrent “system”, or making something multi-threaded when it’s not. But in other ways, in an interview, it boils down to just a piece of code using some concurrency primitives that the OS provides. Is it a design question that doesn’t clearly fit into design category? Maybe. * Take Object Modeling as another example. It is also a “system design” question many would argue, but in an interview, it often boils down to writing a few classes augmented by some diagrams, if at all. So that could be another example. * Take the interview question of Designing Amazon’s Product Review System. On the face of it, it’s probably not even possible to tell what the interviewer is expecting (class design? architecture? UI?). Once you clarify, you may find, that s/he is expecting actual code! And when you start thinking about it, you’ll realize that it boils down to a well-known caching algorithm! So there you go - yet another example. I could go on and on. The point I want to make though, is that it doesn’t really help thinking this way Interviews questions are just that viz. interview questions. Their purpose is to know your thought process, your articulation, your behavioral traits and verify your knowledge/experience. Whether the question comes disguised as a “system design” question or a “coding” question or whatever else, has little relevance. In our programs, we go deep into various CS topics, which eventually helps tremendously in cracking at top companies and sustaining there]

Question: In a coding interview, if you say things like "I don't quite remember the syntax, but…" or "I don't quite know how it is implemented, but…", and is able to provide an answer in plain English and logic, how would the interviewer look upon that?
Answer: Any reasonable interviewer will be fine with that, given you’re not habitually doing it. If you happen to answer like that every time I ask you to go deeper into something, then it starts to get suspicious. If you claim to know one programming language, then I expect that you have an urge to be precise when you express (code) in that language. Notice I didn’t say I expect you to be precise - just an urge to be precise. In other words, it’s very okay to not remember syntax (that’s what IDEs are for), but it’s not okay to just assume that I’ll be fine with it, and move on without checking with me. I need to see you trying to remember syntax and assume a reasonably correct syntax before taking my permission to move on. Handwaving and assuming my agreement is a red flag. It is very okay to not remember how something is implemented, but it’s not okay to say that for everything and not okay to say that for frequently used fundamental building blocks. e.g if you claim to know C++ STL through your work experience, but don’t know that std::map and std::set are implemented with Tree-like access characteristics, then that’s a problem. One very important thing interviewers look for in an interviewee, is an urge to go deeper and have only a few black boxes in systems they use. If the knowledge is surface level only, then it’s usually not very impressive. Especially at top companies. I run a bootcamp, focused on technical interview prep: Interview Kickstart. Previously, I was a Director of Engineering at Box.

Question: What are the best tips for negotiating a compensation package at Google? What should someone know about the way these aspects of compensation will be paid out? What are typical baselines for a program manager and how negotiable are these terms?
Answer: We often negotiate Google offers for candidates from our programs. Here is what we have learnt: 1. Google DOES negotiate. It absolutely does. I respect Bob See’s perspective, but from what we have seen, lately Google has started to budge. They are losing a lot of engineers to Uber and Snapchat, which has made them realize that they need to up their game. 2. Google does not negotiate, if offers are from random-ass companies. In order to move the needle at Google, you need to have competing offers. Good, competing offers from public companies, or pre-IPO companies. Think Uber, Facebook. 3. It depends a LOT on your recruiter. Some recruiters are very seasoned, and they play this psychological war very well. It’s very difficult to negotiate if you are caught with one of those. But other recruiters are more vulnerable. 4. They DO sign on bonuses. Hefty ones sometimes. Sign-on bonuses only happen when you have had a great interview, you get an exceptional fit with a team, and thus they REALLY want to attract you. It doesn’t happen otherwise. 5. Google CAN play evil. Yes, despite their motto. It’s rare, but it does happen. We once had an offer made at Level 3 for a candidate who was on the cusp of 3 and 4. The candidate declined, because they had other better offers (Uber, Dropbox) at higher levels. Despite having full knowledge of other competing offers, Google waited until last minute, and only then offered Level 4, with the condition that the candidate sign the new offer as is, or they will be barred forever from interviewing with Google. You guessed it - it was a seasoned recruiter. In summary, if you have no competing offers from proper companies, and you really want Google, then you are pretty much at the mercy of your recruiter. They might move a bit if you persist and insist, but not much. In order to get something more meaningful out of them you need a strong competing offer. And a degree in psychology if your recruiter is seasoned.

Question: What’s the financial difference between my offers from Google and Uber? Uber has offered me 2100 stocks a year, and Google has offered $70K stocks a year.
Answer: If you really want to understand the economic difference between these two offers, then you need to look at the full picture; not just equity: If you are only interested in equity for some reason, then you have to dig more: Uber: 2100 shares: If your Uber share is worth $33.3, then it’ll be equivalent to Google’s offer (simple calculation of 70k/2100). At $33.3, Uber will be worth about 33B (from your information, it has nearly 1B outstanding shares, give or take, and that is correct from our experience too). Do you think Uber can fetch $33B in valuation when it exits? Chances are healthy because its yearly revenue is more than that (learned thru grapevine). What says that valuation will hold to at least 1x revenue? There is no rule/rhyme/reason for that. Market basis it on growth rate and precedence. Usually, fast-growing companies are worth way more than that. Think 5x or 10x revenues. 1x is generally for slow-growing companies. Google: $70k worth of RSUs: Who says that the RSUs are going to hold value? They may go higher or lower, depending on myriad factors. Given it’s Google though (one of the most innovative companies), you can reasonably assume that it’ll hold value in the vicinity. But that’s about it. That’s pretty much how far you can get when comparing equity. I don’t believe it gives you enough picture though. To get a better picture, you need to examine all aspects of compensation, most importantly what are your growth prospects. After all, you’re going to be spending next several years of your life at one of these places. Hit me up if you have followup questions.

Question: Should I prepare for the interview or build something I like?
Answer: If you are in the final year of MS CS, then I’m assuming that your primary goal is to find your job first. (If you have student loans or are on a visa, then that becomes all the more important). If that is not true, and you want to be an entrepreneur right away, then obviously you should build something. If however your primary goal is to find a job first, then you are better off pursuing a path that has higher chances of leading you to a job. i.e. preparing for interviews. Building a side project can definitely lead to a job, but that assumes a few things: Wanting many things is natural and human. Everyone wants to do many things. People who truly succeed, are the ones who know how to prioritize. That ruthless prioritization is what leads to focus.

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: Why do Microsoft software engineers tend to stay for a long time compared to other tech companies?
Answer: Steven Grimm and John L. Miller have nailed it. Here is one more (supplementing) reason (assuming you interviewed in Seattle WA and are comparing to what you've heard of Bay Area): The culture there is simply not like Bay Area. In the Bay, the socially acceptable maximum to stay at a company has been steadily reducing over the years. These days, it's about 4-6 years, based on my experience. i.e. if you stayed somewhere longer than 6-7 years, you should expect that someone will ask you about it. (If you have steady career progression to show during those years, it's an easy explanation) Why is that? Probably because there are just so many options here. Or probably because startups here come and go so frequently, that it has become socially acceptable to be hopping. When you meet people socially here, you'll have 20 different companies represented in a party of 20 people . (It'd be 4 or 5 in Seattle). And, the next time you meet them, they'll likely be working for some other company, because the first one folded. This makes you think if you're doing the right thing staying longer at your employer. Prediction: It's going to change for Microsoft too. Seattle is changing, so is Microsoft and the concept of long careers is dwindling. Big companies are no longer safe havens for a long career.

Question: Why do interviewers care so much about algorithm and data structures?
Answer: [Image Courtesy: ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ on Twitter ] For fresh grads, part of your hunch is correct. Because of their lack of production-quality experience, we don’t ask too many language/tool/stack/technology specific questions in technical interviews. And when we do, we don’t expect them to know the nuances like a practitioner would do. But that expected lack of experience with specific tools, is not the reason we ask DS/Algos questions in technical interviews. We ask DS/Algos questions also to experienced engineers. Yes, DS/Algos are rarely coded directly in your daily work - in fact, we categorically know that you’re unlikely to use many of them directly, if ever, in your entire career. In fact, if I simply want you to sort a dataset at work, I’d categorically expect you to not code Quicksort in 30 minutes. I’d instead expect you to start with SQL or Command line, and I’ll give time for you to learn it, if you don’t already know it. But, knowing all that fully well, we still ask DS/Algos questions in interviews. That is because technical interviews follow a very different set of constraints and allowances, when compared to actual work. While no interview questions are perfect (much less DS/Algos) and no single type of questions are ever used in isolation, asking DS/Algos questions has numerous advantages to the company, and has important advantages to the candidates (e.g. they let you switch your domain). Following is a relatively long multi-part treatise, explaining this approach. This has been received very well by hundreds of candidates from the course as well as my other speaking engagements. If you have not thought about this before, you may find several useful insights at inconspicuous places below. I hope that it’ll be an interesting read, and worth your time. First of all, pat yourself on the back for asking this question. So many engineers agonize about DS/Algos in interviews, but never once stop to ask this question: why is it such a central part of interviews nowadays? Just trying to answer this question puts you miles ahead of competition. Due to my profession, I breathe technical interviewing. I’ve been asked these questions in my interviews, I have myself asked DS/Algos questions as a hiring manager at Box and before, I’ve helped tech companies set detailed interview processes, I’ve helped head-hunters screen candidates and I’ve also helped candidates do well in such a process. —— 0. The precursor The precursor to DS/Algos types questions, as you may already know, are puzzles and brain-teasers. Puzzles have long been a part of “tradition of tech interviewing”, if I may call it so. A really good introduction to this history, is found in the seminal book How would you move mount Fuji?. Quoting from pages 6 and 7 of that book: “Logic puzzles, riddles, hypothetical questions, and trick questions have a long tradition in computer-industry interviews. This is an expression of the start-up mentality in which every employee is expected to be a highly logical and motivated innovator, working seventy-hour weeks if need be to ship a product. It reflects the belief that the high-technology industries are different from the old economy: less stable, less certain, faster changing. The high-technology employee must be able to question assumptions and see things from novel perspectives. Puzzles and riddles (so the argument goes) test that ability.” —- While that sheds some light on what the origin was, it still leaves the picture incomplete. At least to me. There need to be some distinct advantages to the process, for it to be so prevalent. And there are. I’ll try and enumerate those below, wearing my Hiring Manager (VP Engineering) hat: 1. They fit the best known method of interviewing, very well Interviews, by definition, are supposed to be a predictor of future performance at work. But humans are not that simple. Same person behaves differently in different contexts at different times, rendering most predictions useless. In fact, being “predictable” goes against the most fundamental evolutionary goal of survival. Humans wanted to remain unpredictable, so that they won’t be hunted down. For a long time now, it has been known, that interviews in general, in any field, are a poor predictor of future job performance. See some pointers to that research here: Should we stop interviewing people? Here is some more reinforcement of that, from the horse’s mouth: Google’s SVP of HR talking about their interviewing: Even Google Doesn't Do Interviews Better “We looked at tens of thousands of interviews, and everyone who had done the interviews and what they scored the candidate, and how that person ultimately performed in their job. We found zero relationship. It’s a complete random mess…” So what do we do? Can we stop interviewing and start hiring randomly? No, we cannot, because however sub-optimal the act is, it at least gives us, the hiring managers, a mental satisfaction of trying our best. Trying hence is the keyword. In that spirit, the question really is - what is the best we can do? In other words, what do I test in an interview, such that it gives me the highest possible confidence in predicting your future performance? To answer that question, here is the most relevant and comprehensive meta-research: http://mavweb.mnsu.edu/howard/Schmidt%20and%20Hunter%201998%20Validity%20and%20Utility%20Psychological%20Bulletin.pdf “This article summarizes the practical and theoretical implications of 85 years of research in personnel selection. On the basis of meta-analytic findings, this article presents the validity of 19 selection procedures for predicting job performance and training performance and the validity of paired combinations of general mental ability (GMA) and the 18 other selection procedures. Overall, the 3 combinations with the highest multivariate validity and utility for job performance were GMA plus a work sample test (mean validity of .63), GMA plus an integrity test (mean validity of .65), and GMA plus a structured interview (mean validity of .63). “ In other words, if I don’t ask you some challenging questions (testing GMA), and make sure you also know how to write code (Work Sample), in a structured manner, then my interview of you is merely a coin-toss. DS/Algos questions fit that bill nicely. They can be constructed to be as challenging or as easy as required, to get a good read on your preparation. They can be evaluated more objectively, and they also show your abilities of what you’re going to do at work (write code). If we compare those with other types of questions, the fitment becomes more clear: e.g. Knowledge-based questions (e.g. Java), while can be argued as work-sample tests, they don’t really test the GMA, and are difficult at best to make new/challenging. Also, Software engineering is not a knowledge-based role - it’s a problem-solving role. if companies want to hire knowledge-based roles, they generally just hire contractors. IQ tests are difficult to administer and are not socially acceptable. Heck, even puzzles and riddles are going away from social acceptability. Questions on your past experience are necessary to ask, but not sufficient and like we noticed in the research, they are not a good predictor of future performance. Questions on designing systems similar to what you’re going to design at work, are a close second, and we use them a lot too, but it’s very tedious to get enough variety in them. Plus they are subjective as hell. Note, that as a candidate too, you want to fit into the company, as much as the company wants you to fit in. So you want the company to pick the best possible method of evaluating your candidacy. —— 2. They make it very convenient for companies to interview at scale . Very. When it comes to most good tech companies, you have to realize a couple of things: First: They are not just interviewing. They are interviewing at scale. They are flushed with resumes to the tune of hundreds a day. Second: Interviewing is not anyone’s favorite thing. Spending time on interviewing is the last thought ever. Most engineers don’t ever want to spend time in interviewing. Most of the attention and time at work, is spent in building features and products and shipping them out the door. Interviewing is a necessary evil, at best. There is an entire department for Hiring, but not for interviewing. They are not the same thing. Yes, there are people and pockets who will tell you otherwise. But the moment it comes to getting their bonuses, it’ll be on how many features shipped, not how many engineers interviewed. Maybe in one or two quarters of crunch, the department will encourage more interviewing, but you’re kidding yourselves if you think they are giving it more attention than absolutely minimally necessary. Regardless of their lip-service. Turns out, DS/Algos questions are a boon to companies, when it comes to scaling an interview process with minimal time spent. Let’s see how: * It’s very easy to train the interviewers on them In fact, no formal training is necessary. Pick up any random book or website, read the question, read the answer and deliver it. Also, interviewers only need to get good at just a few questions, maybe 2 to 5. Then they can interview for months together, without knowing or getting good at anything outside that comfort zone. Not fair, you say? Of course, but fairness is not the goal. Goal is to spend least amount of time, not to prove whether it’s fair or not. * They make it easy to evaluate and compare candidates quickly The answers are so closed ended, that it doesn’t need a long debate to tell which candidate did better on reversing a string. And remember, if both candidates don’t cut it, then there are new candidates all the time! * They make it easy to standardize and centralize the process Now you’re not limited to engineers from a certain team to interview members of that team. Whoever is available, can come and do the interview. You can also do rotations of interviewers, so that a select few are not burdened. And of course, you can just create a question bank, so others can pick from there. Not fair you say? Yep, not the goal. See above. —— 3. DS/Algos questions afford great flexibility in the interview room When it’s 1x1 time, they have distinct advantages: * They can be made arbitrarily easy or arbitrarily hard. On the fly Candidate not doing well? Dumb it down to make them feel better. Candidate doing very well? Keep throwing constraints and making it more challenging. Want to get more collaborative with the candidate? DS/Algos questions can be easily morphed into those too! * They can be administered in any writing mode Whiteboarding? Check. Want to write on a piece of paper? Check? Use your own computer? Check? Use an online IDE? Check. Take home exams? Check. These questions are small enough that they can be very flexibly delivered by the company, in any mode you like. * They are agnostic to candidate’s past Isn’t it amazing when you can free the candidate from their past and just have them showcase their skills? Schools, pedigree - why should all that matter? * They avoid storytellers, lets companies hire problem-solvers There is no time for story-telling in a DS/Algos interview. Either you can think and code, or you cannot. It’s that clear. * They can bring out candidate’s behavior when challenged This is subtle, and often overlooked. But when I challenge a candidate on something hard, whether they succeed or not, but how they handle that tells a lot about them. Do they take hints when I give them? Are they respectful? Is their head firmly in solving the problem, or do they get distracted? Do they give up? Those are immensely valuable traits to know, which don’t come out any other way. —- 4. They are candidate friendly! Don’t believe me? For candidates, here are some invaluable advantages in this approach: * They let you switch your technical domain! Right? If you are coming from X domain and I want you for Y, how else will I know, that you’re a good software engineer? As an interviewer, I know nothing about your domain, and you know nothing about mine. Where the hell do we meet? DS/Algos questions provide that lowest common denominator. Otherwise if you worked in Payment systems in your first job, you’ll hole yourselves to that, all your programming career. * Now you’re not stuck to your programming language! If you are a Java programmer, you can continue to interview in Java, even though my shop may be doing PHP. I understand, that good engineers rise above languages, and this lets you have that chance to write code in something you know well. Otherwise, good luck switching to a new stack, ever! * You can truly prepare for technical interviews! YES! Companies scream at the top of their voices, for you to not come to the interviews without preparation. They send you prep material, recommend books and courses! They are not stupid! Go back to reason #2. Interviews are not their favorite thing to do and suck a lot of time out of more important things. As an interviewer, I’d much rather compare two prepared candidates, than suffer thru an ill-prepared candidate. That’s because I know what I’m looking for - your preparation is not going to cloud my judgment in an incorrect way. I understand, that it’s up to me, and I want you to prepare, so as to respect my time in the interview. e.g. If I ask you a Graphs question and you fumble thru a BFS/DFS implementation, there is nothing more frustrating and boring than that. I’d much rather see you fly thru it, and then discuss tradeoffs of different solutions. —- 5. Downsides of this process are not that big for anyone Following are some downsides to having DS/Algos questions in the interview process. But notice that none of these are unique to these questions, or wild. They are relatively easy to address: * Downside: Interviewers still have to know what to look for Asking DS/Algos questions can quickly devolve into a game of finding the best answer. But that’s not the right thing to look for. Right thing to do, is to pay attention to the thought process (more on this in a different answer). This however, does come around with experience. Once you do a few interviews, you’ll naturally calibrate yourself to look for what matters. * Downside: Candidate performance on these questions is equally dependent on interviewERs In other words, if you take someone thru a set of 5 engineers in a company, there is no guarantee that they will do well with another 5 people in the same company. Another way of saying this, is that beyond a certain preparation level, your interview depends on the interviewERs as much as it depends on your preparation. That sucks for candidates, but it’s OKAY for companies, because they have enough information to call your candidacy, with whichever set of people interviews you. If you clear one panel, then they will find sufficient documentable reason (read: excuse) to hire you. And remember, they have to hire. So they won’t put you thru another ringer! * Downside: Lots of false negatives There are many candidates who don’t know about the process, or who fail to prepare, or who just outright reject to be subjected to these. Among those, there are many good candidates (false negatives) that the company is losing. But you know what, companies don’t care much about losing false negatives, because they have a steady supply of people who are happy preparing for and going thru this process! Also note that none of these downsides are unique to DS/Algos based interview process. In fact, there is no perfect interview process. For candidates, the only “downside” is that they have to prepare. That can be annoying, but when done right, it can be very very enjoyable, and you’ll learn a lot. We know that, because many candidates come to the course with no intent to even look for a job. That, according to my subjective belief, is the hallmark of a good course. —- 6. When not to use DS/Algos questions This section is strictly not a reason per se, but the reasoning is not complete without understanding when we shouldn’t use them. * Don’t use them when you’re not interviewing at scale Hiring for only 1 or 2 positions a quarter? Don’t have a pipeline like the hot tech companies do? Rethink your process. You have time to pay attention to build a more tailor-made process for your role and the type of person you’re seeking. Don’t just blindly emulate the top places. * Don’t use them for candidates whose reputation precedes them If the candidate has something to show for e.g. a popular open-source project that you’re trying to hire for, try to get a better idea of their current skills by doing some design questions with them. * Don’t use them on candidates with direct domain experience Once in a while, you see a candidate who has done exactly what you want them to do in the team. If you can reasonably say, that you will want that role for the foreseeable future to stay as is, then structure the interview very precisely to that domain. * Don’t use them, if you don’t appreciate them, or understand them I’ve been told of many instances when the interviewers have delivered questions despite not knowing how to solve it themselves. That’s just evil and incompetent. Don’t ever do that. You’ll not inspire good people to join you if you do that. I hope I can make you see, that while DS/Algos questions are not the best or only question-type used in technical interviews, in grand scheme of things, they are the most convenient from multiple perspectives, and hence have found their groove. Convenience - Isn’t that how life works most of the time anyway? :-) - Soham Coding Interview Preparation Bootcamp
